newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: China slams Manila airstrip in Spratlys.
newsitem.headline: China slams Manila airstrip in Spratlys.

text.p: China on Monday criticised the Philippines for opening an airstrip on one of the disputed Spratly Islands but Manila said it was merely upgrading supply lines to its troops there and not building a new garrison.
The Chinese Embassy said in a statement China "enjoys indisputable sovereignty" over the South China Sea islands and urged the Philippines not to take any action that would harm relations.

Philippine armed forces chief General Arnulfo Acedera inaugurated the 1.3 km (0.8 mile) long airstrip on one of the islands in the Kalayaan island group during a Christmas Day visit to Filipino soldiers in the area.

Acedera said in a statement on Monday he went to Kalayaan mainly "to bring Christmas cheers to the troops" and also to re-open an existing but renovated airstrip. He denied newspaper reports that the Philippines planned to set up a new garrison in Kalayaan.

Besides visiting the soldiers "deployed in the most isolated and loneliest assignment...the visit was to officially re-open the rehabilitated runway...which has not been operational for quite a time due to some eroded portions," Acedera said.
"The AFP (Armed Forces of the Philippines) does not intend to build a new military garrison in the area," he added.

"Rather, the military plans to upgrade its facilities in the island to support requirements of some government agencies and other non-governmental organisations in pursuit of their scientific research studies."

Chinese President Jiang Zemin and Philippine President Fidel Ramos agreed during Jiang's visit to Manila last month to shelve differences over the Spratlys and consider cooperation in developing the area.

Manila claims ownership of the eight-island Kalayaan group in the Spratlys. The cluster of potentially oil-rich but largely uninhabited isles, shoals and reefs are claimed wholly or in part by China, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei.

Tensions between Manila and Beijing flared last year after China built structures on one of the islands that Manila said could be used as naval support facilities. Beijing says the structures are shelters for fishermen.
A military spokesman said about 50 to 60 Philippine soldiers were deployed in some of the areas claimed by Manila, most of them in Pagasa, the biggest in the Kalayaan group.
Presidential Executive Secretary Ruben Torres denied the Philippines was engaged in a military buildup in Kalayaan.
"We are there to be able to supply our original forces there. We are not increasing the forces. What we are doing is to improve the supply lines," Torres told reporters.
He said the Department of Foreign Affairs was studying the Chinese embassy statement.
Chinese Embassy spokesman Hao Yinpiao said no official protest had been lodged with the Philippine government.
"They should refrain from any move to harm bilateral relations," Hao said by telephone.
"What we are hoping for is that both sides should abide by the principles the state leaders have reached," he added, referring to the agreement between Ramos and Jiang.
